When something calls forth something else, it causes it to come out — from inside a person, a situation, or the world — often something that was hidden, sleeping, or waiting to appear.

Think of it this way: imagine courage sitting quietly inside a soldier. Then a great battle begins. The battle doesn't create the courage from nothing — it pulls it out, brings it to the surface. That is what "call forth" means. The battle called forth the soldier's courage.

• Call = to summon; to cause something to come
  • Forth = forward; out into the open

Put them together: call forth = to cause something to move forward and out into the open, from a hidden or inactive state.

The word "forth" is old and formal. You don't hear it much in modern conversation ("come forth," "go forth," "bring forth"), but you do find it in writing, speeches, and literature — and "call forth" belongs to that formal, slightly elevated style.

"Call forth" has two closely related uses:

Use 1 — To cause a feeling, quality, or response to emerge

This is by far the most common use. Something — an event, a person, a situation, a piece of art — triggers something that was latent (= present but inactive) inside a person or a group.

The thing that is "called forth" is usually:

  • An emotion: courage, fear, admiration, grief, anger, love
  • A quality or ability: strength, creativity, resilience, the best in someone
  • A response or reaction: protests, applause, sympathy, controversy
  • A memory or image: a childhood scene, a feeling from the past

The general's speech called forth enormous courage in his soldiers.

(The speech triggered/evoked the courage that was already inside them.)

Her kindness called forth deep gratitude in everyone around her.

The film called forth memories of my childhood that I had long forgotten.

The government's decision called forth widespread protest across the country.

Use 2 — To summon someone or something to come forward (formal/literary)

In older or more literary language, "call forth" can mean to summon someone — to command or invite them to step forward or appear.

The king called forth his bravest knights.

In the story, the magician called forth a spirit from the shadows.

This second use is less common in modern writing and mostly appears in historical texts, fiction, or poetic language.
The Key Insight: Something Already There

One of the most important things to understand about "call forth" is this:

What is called forth is usually already there — it just needed something to bring it out.

You don't call forth something created from nothing. You call forth something that was inside, dormant, or potential. The trigger (the event, the person, the situation) acts like a key that unlocks it.

This is what makes "call forth" slightly different from just "create" or "cause." It carries the sense of drawing out something that existed but was not yet visible or active.
Grammar: How to Use It in a Sentence

"Call forth" is a transitive phrasal verb, which means it always needs an object — something that gets called forth.

Structure: Subject + call forth + object

The crisis called forth the best in people.
(Subject = the crisis; object = the best in people)

Her smile called forth a warmth in him he had never felt before.

It is separable, meaning the object can sometimes go between "call" and "forth":

The music called old memories forth.

(Less common, but grammatically correct)

The situation called something remarkable forth in her.

However, when the object is a pronoun (it, them, him, her), it must go between "call" and "forth":

✅ The crisis called it forth.
❌ The crisis called forth it. (wrong)

Tip: In most cases, it is more natural and common to say "call forth + [object]" — keeping "forth" right after "call," especially in writing.
Register: When Is This Phrase Used?

"Call forth" is formal and literary. You will find it in:

  • Essays and academic writing
  • Speeches and political language
  • Literature, novels, and poetry
  • Journalism and editorial writing
  • Historical texts

You would not usually say it in casual conversation. A friend would more naturally say:

"The movie brought out a lot of emotions in me."

rather than:

"The movie called forth a lot of emotions in me."

Both are correct — but "call forth" signals a more elevated, serious, or literary tone. Knowing this helps you use it appropriately and also recognize it when you read it.
How It Differs from Similar Phrases

"Bring out" — the everyday, neutral version of "call forth." Same basic idea, but much more common in conversation. "Call forth" is more dramatic and formal.

"Evoke" — a single-word verb that means almost exactly the same thing as "call forth" in Use 1. "The music evoked memories" = "The music called forth memories." "Evoke" is also formal, but slightly more common in modern writing.

"Call up" — can also mean to bring memories to mind ("it called up old images"), but "call up" has additional meanings (like calling someone on the phone, or calling soldiers into military service), so it is more ambiguous. "Call forth" is cleaner and more precise when you mean evoking something.

"Summon" — similar to Use 2 of "call forth" (commanding someone to appear). "Summon" is more about an authoritative command; "call forth" can be gentler or more poetic.

Picture something buried underground, like a seed. Nothing happens to it for a long time. Then rain comes. The rain does not create the flower — it calls the flower forth from the seed. It draws it out, brings it forward, makes it emerge.

That image — of something latent being drawn outward into the world — is the heart of "call forth."

"Call forth" means to cause something — especially a feeling, quality, memory, or response — to emerge and come into expression, often from a hidden or inactive state inside a person or group; in more literary use, it can also mean to summon someone or something to come forward.
